title: Fewest Sprinklers to Soak a Lawn
statement:
A lawn is the line segment from point 0 to point n. There is a sprinkler at every whole point 0, 1, …, n. Sprinkler i has reach ranges[i]: when it is on, it soaks the segment [i − ranges[i], i + ranges[i]]. A sprinkler with reach 0 soaks only its own point, which covers no length.

Return the smallest number of sprinklers to turn on so that the whole segment [0, n] is soaked. Segments that only touch at an end point still join up. If the lawn cannot be fully soaked, return -1.

examples.why: Sprinkler 1 soaks [−1, 3], sprinkler 4 soaks [2, 6], sprinkler 7 soaks [6, 8]. Nothing that covers 0 reaches past 3, so two are not enough.
Sprinkler 1 covers [−2, 4] and sprinkler 5 covers [3, 7]. Spray past the ends of the lawn is fine.
The two end sprinklers soak [0, 1] and [3, 4]. Nothing covers the stretch from 1 to 3.

hints: Each sprinkler is an interval. Only its left end (clamped to 0) and right end (clamped to n) matter.
For every left point, keep only the furthest right end that starts there. Now it looks like jumping along the lawn: from what you have covered so far, how far can one more sprinkler take you?

Sweep left to right like the fewest-jumps game: track the end of the current cover and the furthest reach among intervals starting inside it. When you hit the current end, you must add a sprinkler and jump to the furthest reach. If that reach does not move forward, return -1.

explain.intuition:
Convert each sprinkler into an interval [max(0, i − r), min(n, i + r)]. Out of all intervals that start at the same point, only the one reaching furthest right is useful, so record reach[left] = furthest right end.

Now it is the fewest-jumps problem. Say everything up to end is covered with count sprinklers. Among all intervals that start at or before end, pick the one reaching furthest. Picking anything shorter can never help, because any later choice from the shorter cover is also available from the longer one. When the sweep reaches end, add a sprinkler and move end to the best reach seen. If the best reach is not past end, there is a dry gap.
steps: Build reach of size n + 1: for each i with r = ranges[i], set reach[max(0, i − r)] = max(that, min(n, i + r)).
If p == end: when far ≤ p return -1; otherwise increase count and set end = far.
pitfalls: Forgetting to clamp the left end to 0. A sprinkler at 1 with reach 3 starts covering at 0, not at −2, and must be found when the sweep is at 0.
Counting a sprinkler with reach 0 as covering its point. It covers no length, so it never closes a gap.
Picking the sprinkler with the largest reach overall first. Large reach in the wrong place can leave gaps that cost more sprinklers.

solutions.title: DP over covered prefix
solutions.idea: best[x] = fewest sprinklers that soak [0, x]. An interval [l, r] lets every point in (l, r] be reached with best[l] + 1.
solutions.time: O(n · R) where R is the largest reach

solutions.title: Furthest reach per start, then fewest jumps
solutions.idea: Keep only the longest interval starting at each point and sweep like the fewest-jumps game.

followups: Return which sprinklers to turn on, not just how many.
Sprinklers can be anywhere on the line, given as arbitrary intervals. What replaces the reach array? (Hint: sort by start.)
